title: Sushi Sits Beside Chaat at Delhi's Dussehra Melas This Festival Season
excerpt: India Today found sushi served alongside chaat and pav bhaji at Delhi's Ramlila fairs, where the traditional stalls — chaat, jalebis and kulfi at Subhash Maidan — still anchor the mela menu.
body:
• India Today reported sushi being served alongside chaat and pav bhaji at Delhi's Dussehra melas this year — a Japanese staple taking a stall next to the festival's street-food regulars.
  • The traditional core has not moved: at Subhash Maidan near the Red Fort, stalls still centre on chaat, jalebis and kulfi, with Chandni Chowk crawls adding hot jalebis, chaat and Mughlai food.
  • Delhi's Ramlila season runs October 11-21, with Ravan Dahan on Dussehra, October 20; the Red Fort venues are easiest by metro to Lal Quila on the Violet Line.
  • For diaspora readers planning a Delhi trip or comparing notes with US Navratri food stalls, the mela menu is a useful snapshot of how festival food in India now mixes the familiar with the imported.

At Delhi's Dussehra melas this year, the queue tells the story. Alongside the chaat counters and pav bhaji stalls that have defined the Ramlila fair for generations, vendors are serving sushi — India Today reported — placing a Japanese restaurant staple in the middle of a North Indian religious fair.

The headline writes itself — sushi as the new chaat, almost — but the qualifier matters. Nothing in the mela's traditional food economy has been displaced. What has changed is the width of the menu a family expects to find between the Ferris wheel and the Ramlila stage.

The mela the sushi landed in

Delhi's Ramlila celebrations run through October, with Dussehra on October 20 and Ravan Dahan that evening. Outlook Traveller's guide to the 2026 season lists celebrations from October 11 to 21, led by the Lav Kush Ramlila at the Red Fort grounds — known for large stages, elaborate sets and celebrity appearances — where visitors explore the surrounding mela, with food stalls and festive attractions adding to the atmosphere.

At the Shri Dharmik Lila Committee's grounds at Subhash Maidan, opposite the Old Lajpat Rai Market near the Red Fort, Outlook Traveller describes the surrounding food stalls as an important part of the experience: visitors stop for chaat, jalebis, kulfi and other festive treats while exploring the mela, in what it calls a taste of Old Delhi's food culture. Her Zindagi's Dussehra guide makes the same point about Subhash Maidan, pairing traditional Ravan Dahan with Chandni Chowk street food crawls including hot jalebis, chaat and Mughlai feasts. The full venue guide is at Outlook Traveller.

"What has changed is the width of the menu a family expects to find between the Ferris wheel and the Ramlila stage."

Why sushi fits the fair, on paper

A mela stall has always rewarded food that is quick to assemble, easy to eat standing up and bought in small, shareable portions. Chaat built its dominance on exactly those terms. Sushi rolls meet the same test in a different register: bite-sized, made to order at a counter, and familiar now to a generation of Delhi diners who encounter Japanese food in malls and delivery apps rather than only in hotels. Pav bhaji, the third item in India Today's pairing, is itself an import that became a street staple — a Mumbai dish that Delhi fairs absorbed long ago.

The pattern is absorption, not replacement. Delhi's festival grounds have repeatedly taken an outside dish, put it on a paper plate and made it fair food. Sushi is simply the newest arrival at a fair whose centre — the Ramayana on stage, the effigies of Ravana, Meghnada and Kumbhakarna waiting for the evening — has not changed.

The wider fair

The food sits inside a much larger production. Her Zindagi's guide lists venues from the Dwarka Sector 10 grounds, with a 221-foot Ravana effigy described as India's tallest, to the Punjabi Bagh Ramlila Ground with its carnival rides and family enclosures, and the DDA Ground at Netaji Subhash Place in Pitampura, with spacious seating and food stalls next to the metro station. Outlook Traveller advises taking the metro — Lal Quila on the Violet Line for the Red Fort venues, Dwarka Sector 10 on the Blue Line for Dwarka — arriving early, and leaving time for the food, with queues expected at the Old Delhi stalls.

What diaspora readers will recognise

Indian-American festival-goers will recognise the dynamic. Navratri and Diwali fairs in the United States went through the same widening years ago, when stalls that once served only samosas and jalebis added noodles, pizza and fusion chaat to hold younger crowds. Delhi's melas are now making the same calculation at a far larger scale — and sushi, of all things, is the marker that the calculation has gone fully global.

What's next

The season closes with Ravan Dahan on October 20 and mela activity running to October 21 at the Red Fort venues. Whether sushi returns next Dussehra will depend on the only verdict a fair recognises: whether the stall held its queue against the chaat counter next door. On this year's evidence, it has earned the chance.
